newsitem.title: DENMARK: Maersk challenges SAS on Stockholm route.
newsitem.headline: Maersk challenges SAS on Stockholm route.

text.p: Danish airline Maersk Air on Thursday announced the launch of regular flights between Copenhagen and Stockholm, the latest challenge to Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) domination of the region's airspace.
Maersk, owned by shipping and energy group A.P. Moeller, said it would start the new service on April 28, in cooperation with Finland's Finnair.
"Maersk Air and Finnair will each have four departures daily each way on the Copenhagen-Stockholm route on weekdays," Maersk Air managing director Bjarne Hansen said at a news conference.
"There will also be a few weekend flights," Hansen added.
A joint statement said that Maersk and Finnair would share codes and airport handling and offer cheaper fares than SAS, with fewer restrictions.
SAS, owned jointly by the Danish, Norwegian and Swedish governments and private investors, said it was not alarmed by the fresh competition although it took it seriously.

"We have known for quite a while that Maersk and Finnair were planning to compete with us on the Copenhagen-Stockholm route .... it's nothing new, so we are ready for them," spokesman Troels Rasmussen told Reuters.

"SAS has learnt a lot on price strategy and service from competing with Braathens on the Stockholm-Oslo route. We have came out best there. We are well prepared but I want to make it quite clear that we consider Maersk and Finnair to be serious competitors," Rasmussen said.
Norwegian group Braathens SAFE last November launched regular flights between Oslo and Stockholm, one of SAS' most profitable routes, and plans further expansion.
The Norwegian firm, which shares a frequent-flyer programme with British Airways, has bought half of Swedish domestic airline Transwede and intends to acquire the rest.

Danish short-haul outfit Sun-Air took on BA colours last May as a holder of the British Airways Express franchise, offering flights from Copenhagen and Aarhus to Oslo, Gothenburg and Stockholm and declaring war on SAS regional dominance.
"We hope this franchise arrangement with Sun-Air is a small start to the end of such dominance," BA Area Manager Lee Shave said at the time.

Aviation insiders have said that BA appeared to be positioning itself for a major assault on SAS. Maersk itself is linked to the British giant through its British-based Maersk Air Ltd., which is also a British Airways Express franchisee.
One of BA's bitterest rivals is also looking for a slice of the Scandinavian pie.
British tycoon Richard Branson's Virgin Express started flights between Copenhagen and its Brussels base last autumn and is openly eyeing the Copenhagen-Oslo-Stockholm triangle.

SAS reported a 41 percent fall in pre-tax profits for the first nine months of 1996 and has cancelled six international routes as part of an extensive cost-cutting programme. It says however that it intends to increase passenger volume and market share, helped by its alliance with Germany's Lufthansa.
